# Using lt from JavaScript {#chp:js}

You do not need R to use lt. The whole library is a few small scripts and one
idea: *a table is JSON*. Hand the runtime a spec, get a table back. This
chapter is for people building pages by hand, for apps written in other
languages, and for the curious who want to see what R is quietly writing for
them. Every example below is live: the code is the whole program, and the table
under it is what the browser built from it.

```{r assets, echo = FALSE, results = 'asis'}
# link the runtime (lt-plot loads before the core script)
cat(
  lt:::css_block(c('lt.css', 'lt-plot.css', 'lt-interactive.css'), inline = FALSE),
  lt:::js_block(c('lt-plot.js', 'lt.js', 'lt-interactive.js'), inline = FALSE),
  sep = '\n'
)
```

```{js, echo = FALSE}
// lt.js is deferred: queue LT.build() calls until it loads (other chapters
// may have created window.LT already, so add build() to it)
(window.LT ??= {}).build ??= function(spec) {
  (this.q ??= []).push({s: document.currentScript, d: spec});
};
```

## Including lt.js {#sec:js-include}

A page needs a stylesheet and a script for the core:

``` html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@xiee/utils/css/lt.min.css">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@xiee/utils/js/lt.min.js"></script>
```

Two optional modules sit beside it, and a page pays only for what it uses:

- Interactivity (sorting, search, filters, paging, resizing, and so on) comes
  from `lt-interactive`. Load it *after* the core.
- Inline graphics (error bars, sparklines, dot plots) come from `lt-plot`. Load
  it *before* the core, so its cell renderers are registered by the time the
  runtime builds a table.

``` html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@xiee/utils/css/lt-plot.min.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@xiee/utils/css/lt.min.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@xiee/utils/css/lt-interactive.min.css">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@xiee/utils/js/lt-plot.min.js"></script>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@xiee/utils/js/lt.min.js"></script>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@xiee/utils/js/lt-interactive.min.js"></script>
```

The files are published on npm as `@xiee/utils`. The URLs above track the latest
release; to pin a version, put it after the package name, such as
`@xiee/utils@1.14.154/js/lt.min.js` (use the version you tested with). Server mode
adds one more script, `lt-server.js`; see @sec:server.

Then call `LT.build(spec)` from an inline `<script>` wherever you want a table.
The runtime renders it right after the calling script element. To build a table
at any other time, such as when the reader expands a row, use
`LT.render(element, spec)` instead (@sec:js-render).

If you load the core script with `defer`, as this book does, an inline
`LT.build()` runs before the script arrives. Queue the calls with a tiny shim
placed before them: define `window.LT` with a `build()` that stores
`document.currentScript` and the spec, as the hidden chunk at the top of this
page does. The runtime drains the queue when it loads. Without `defer`, no shim
is needed.

## The anatomy of a spec {#sec:js-spec}

A spec is a plain object. Only `data` is required; everything else decorates it.

:::: {.table #tab:js-spec}
::: caption
[ ](#@tab:js-spec) The top-level keys of a spec.
:::

| Key | What it holds |
|----|----------------------------------------------|
| `data` | An object of columns, each an array of values (`null` for missing). |
| `header` | `{ title, subtitle }`. |
| `spanners` | Labels spanning groups of columns: `[{ label, columns }]`. |
| `row_group` | A column name (separator rows) or an array of column names (rowspan cells). |
| `footnotes` | Numbered notes attached to a title, label, group, or cell. |
| `notes` | Unnumbered source notes below the footnotes. |
| `ops` | The list of operations, applied in order. |
| `interactive` | Switches on sorting, search, filters, and more (@sec:js-interactive). |
| `auto_label`, `auto_format`, `auto_span`, `auto_sep` | Switches for the automatic behaviors. |
| `html_cols`, `class` | Raw-HTML columns and a scoping class. |
::::

The `ops` do the heavy lifting. Each is an object whose `type` names the
operation, and they run in the order given, so format a number *before* you
merge it into a string.

:::: {.table #tab:js-ops}
::: caption
[ ](#@tab:js-ops) The operations, with the section that shows each.
:::

| `type` | Does what |
|----|----------------------------------------------|
| `label`, `align`, `width` | Column labels, alignment, and column or table widths. |
| `fmt_number`, `fmt_date`, `sub` | Format numbers and dates; substitute text for special values. |
| `merge`, `move`, `hide` | Combine, reorder, and hide columns. |
| `row_group`, `group_order`, `indent` | Manual groups, their order, and nesting. |
| `style` | CSS for chosen cells. |
| `errorbar`, `sparkline`, `dotplot` | Inline graphics. |
::::

The easiest way to learn the vocabulary is to let R write it: build a table in
R, call `lt_spec()` (see @sec:spec), and read the JSON.

## Building a table {#sec:js-build}

Put `LT.build(spec)` in a `<script>` where the table should appear. This one has
a title, two formatted columns, and a little interactivity.

```{r, child = ex('js-build')}
```

The sections below take the pieces one at a time. First, sample data. The
examples share two small datasets, filled in from R through litedown's `fill`
option and turned into JavaScript objects:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
iris5 = iris[c(1, 2, 51, 52, 101), ]  # span all three species
mtcars6 = head(mtcars[, 1:6], 6)
```

```{js, fill = xfun::tojson}
const mtcars = `{ mtcars6 }`;
const iris = `{ iris5 }`;
```

### Basic table {#sec:js-basic}

The simplest spec is just `data`, a column-oriented object.

```{js}
LT.build({ data: mtcars });
```

### Title and subtitle {#sec:js-header}

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: iris,
  header: {
    title: "Iris Measurements",
    subtitle: "First five observations"
  }
});
```

### Labels {#sec:js-label}

By default, column names are cleaned for display by replacing `.` and `_` with
spaces, so `Sepal.Length` shows as "Sepal Length". Set `auto_label: false` to
show the raw names, or use a `label` op to name specific columns.

```{js}
// auto_label on by default: "Sepal.Length" displays as "Sepal Length"
LT.build({ data: iris });
```

```{js}
// Disable auto-labeling
LT.build({ data: iris, auto_label: false });
```

```{js}
// Explicit label overrides
LT.build({
  data: iris,
  ops: [
    { type: "label", labels: {
      "Sepal.Length": "Length (cm)", "Sepal.Width": "Width (cm)",
      "Petal.Length": "Length (cm)", "Petal.Width": "Width (cm)"
    }}
  ]
});
```

```{js}
// Disable auto-labeling
LT.build({ data: iris, auto_label: false });
```

### Alignment {#sec:js-align}

Numeric columns are right-aligned and everything else left-aligned. Override
with an `align` op:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: mtcars,
  ops: [
    { type: "align", columns: ["mpg", "cyl"], align: "center" }
  ]
});
```

## Formatting numbers and dates {#sec:js-format}

### Auto-formatting {#sec:js-auto}

Numeric columns format themselves, so a bare `data` already looks decent. The
rules, all visible in this example:

- Values round to about four significant digits, adapting the decimals to the
  magnitude.
- Large numbers get a thin-space thousands separator, and negatives get a
  typographic minus (U+2212).
- A column whose name matches `/%|[ _](pct|percent)$/i` is read as a proportion:
  values are multiplied by 100 and suffixed with "%".
- A column named like `/year/i` holding 4-digit integers is left alone.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Year: [2020, 2021, 2022],
    Revenue: [1234567.89, 2345678.12, -3456.789],
    Margin_pct: [0.1234, 0.0567, 0.2345]
  }
});
```

Set `auto_format: false` to see the raw values instead:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Year: [2020, 2021, 2022],
    Revenue: [1234567.89, 2345678.12, -3456.789],
    Margin_pct: [0.1234, 0.0567, 0.2345]
  },
  auto_format: false
});
```

### Numbers with `fmt_number` {#sec:js-number}

When you want control, a `fmt_number` op sets the decimals and thousands
separator (`big_mark`) per column. Add `percent: true` to multiply by 100 and
append "%".

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Item: ["Widget", "Gadget", "Doohickey"],
    Revenue: [1234567.891, 987654.321, 246913.57],
    Margin: [0.1234, 0.0567, 0.2345]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["Revenue"], decimals: 0, big_mark: "," },
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["Margin"], decimals: 2, percent: true }
  ]
});
```

For columns that span several orders of magnitude, `sig_digits` keeps a fixed
number of significant digits instead of a fixed number of decimals:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Particle: ["Electron", "Proton", "Alpha"],
    Mass: [0.00054858, 1.00727647, 4.00150618]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["Mass"], sig_digits: 3 }
  ]
});
```

If the values are already on the percent scale, use `percent: "%"`, which
appends the sign without multiplying:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Test: ["A", "B"],
    Rate: [78.5, 42.1]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["Rate"], decimals: 1, percent: "%" }
  ]
});
```

`prefix` and `suffix` add currency symbols or units:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Item: ["Widget", "Gadget", "Doohickey"],
    Price: [1234.5, 678.9, 42.0],
    Weight: [1250, 340.5, 89.12]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["Price"], decimals: 2, big_mark: ",", prefix: "$" },
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["Weight"], decimals: 1, suffix: " kg" }
  ]
});
```

### Dates with `fmt_date` {#sec:js-date}

Values can be `Date` objects or ISO strings. By default `fmt_date` calls
`toLocaleDateString()`. Pass `method` to call another `Date` method, or
`locale` and `options` for full `Intl.DateTimeFormat` control.

Mind the time zone. `new Date("2024-01-15")` is parsed as UTC midnight, but
`toLocaleDateString()` converts to local time, so that date shows as
`2024-01-14` for a reader at GMT-6. Pass `options: { timeZone: "UTC" }` to avoid
the shift.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Event: ["Launch", "Update", "Release"],
    Date: [new Date("2024-01-15"), new Date("2024-06-30"), new Date("2024-12-01")]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_date", columns: ["Date"] }
  ]
});
```

A locale and options give you, say, a Chinese long date:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Event: ["Launch", "Update"],
    Date: [new Date("2024-01-15"), new Date("2024-06-30")]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_date", columns: ["Date"], locale: "zh-CN",
      options: { year: "numeric", month: "long", day: "numeric",
                 weekday: "long", timeZone: "UTC" } }
  ]
});
```

Use `method` for a different `Date` method:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Event: ["Launch", "Update"],
    Date: [new Date("2024-01-15"), new Date("2024-06-30")]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_date", columns: ["Date"], method: "toDateString" }
  ]
});
```

For date-times, include the time components in `options`:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Event: ["Start", "End"],
    Time: [new Date("2024-01-15T09:30:00Z"), new Date("2024-01-15T17:45:00Z")]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_date", columns: ["Time"], locale: "en-US",
      options: { year: "numeric", month: "short", day: "numeric",
                 hour: "2-digit", minute: "2-digit" } }
  ]
});
```

### Substituting values with `sub` {#sec:js-sub}

Replace missing, zero, or small values with display text. Put `sub` after the
formatting op so it sees the numbers first.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Metric: ["HR", "p-value", "Events", "Rate"],
    Value: [0.62, 0.0003, 0, null]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["Value"], decimals: 2 },
    { type: "sub", columns: ["Value"], missing: "n/a", zero: "—", small: 0.001, small_text: "< 0.001" }
  ]
});
```

Infinities need a JavaScript object rather than JSON (JSON has no `Infinity`),
and they format as the symbols themselves:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Metric: ["Lower bound", "Upper bound", "Rate", "Missing"],
    Value: [-Infinity, Infinity, 1.5, null]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["Value"], decimals: 2 }
  ]
});
```

## Columns {#sec:js-columns}

### Merging with `merge` {#sec:js-merge}

Combine several columns into one display column. The `pattern` uses `{1}`,
`{2}`, and so on for the columns in order. Wrap a stretch in `<<` and `>>` to
make it conditional: it vanishes when any value inside it is missing, which is
how the tertiary row below loses its empty confidence interval.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Endpoint: ["Primary", "Secondary", "Tertiary"],
    est: [0.61, 0.79, 0.45],
    ci_lo: [0.40, 0.57, null],
    ci_hi: [0.82, 1.01, null]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["est", "ci_lo", "ci_hi"], decimals: 2 },
    { type: "merge", columns: ["est", "ci_lo", "ci_hi"], pattern: "{1}<< ({2}, {3})>>" },
    { type: "label", labels: { est: "Estimate (95% CI)" } }
  ]
});
```

### Spanners {#sec:js-spanner}

A spanner groups contiguous columns under a shared header:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: iris,
  spanners: [
    { label: "Sepal", columns: ["Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width"] },
    { label: "Petal", columns: ["Petal.Length", "Petal.Width"] }
  ]
});
```

Set `auto_span: true` to infer spanners from the column names. Names split on
the first `.` or `_`, contiguous columns sharing a prefix are grouped, and the
labels shrink to the suffix. A string such as `"[.]"` is taken as a regular
expression for a custom separator.

```{js}
LT.build({ data: iris, auto_span: true });
```

### Widths {#sec:js-width}

A `width` op sets column widths with any CSS length:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: mtcars,
  ops: [
    { type: "width", widths: { mpg: "10em", cyl: "5em", disp: "10em", hp: "8em" } }
  ]
});
```

Give it `table` to size the whole table. It combines with column `widths`:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: iris,
  ops: [
    { type: "width", table: "80%" }
  ]
});
```

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: iris,
  ops: [
    { type: "width", table: "100%", widths: { Species: "20em" } }
  ]
});
```

### Moving and hiding {#sec:js-move}

A `move` op puts columns first (`after: null`) or after a named column:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: iris,
  ops: [
    { type: "move", columns: ["Petal.Length", "Petal.Width"], after: null }
  ]
});
```

A `hide` op drops columns from view but not from the spec. Their values still
travel with the row, so anything that reads the whole row, such as an
interactive table's `detail`, can use them.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: iris,
  ops: [
    { type: "hide", columns: ["Petal.Length", "Petal.Width"] }
  ]
});
```

## Inline plots {#sec:js-plots}

Three ops draw small SVG graphics in cells. They come from the graphics module
(`lt-plot.js`, loaded before the core script), and the SVG is built in the
browser from the numbers, so an interactive table draws only the rows on the
current page.

### Error bars {#sec:js-errorbar}

`errorbar` draws a point at the estimate with a bar (and end caps) from the
lower to the upper bound, on a scale shared by the column. `columns` lists the
value column, `lowers` and `uppers` the matching bounds; the plot replaces the
first value column's cells, so hide the bounds. `min` and `max` set the shared
scale, `ref` draws a vertical reference line, and `width` and `height` size each
SVG. `axis: true` adds a shared axis to the footer (ticks and labels at round
values, plus gridlines in the cells), which `axis_label` captions.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Term: ["Age", "Dose", "Baseline", "Sex"],
    Est:  [0.12, -0.34, 0.45, -0.08],
    Lo:   [-0.05, -0.52, 0.21, -0.29],
    Hi:   [0.29, -0.16, 0.69, 0.13]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "hide", columns: ["Lo", "Hi"] },
    { type: "errorbar", columns: ["Est"], lowers: ["Lo"], uppers: ["Hi"],
      min: -0.6, max: 0.7, ref: 0, axis: true, axis_label: "Effect (95% CI)" }
  ]
});
```

Several series stack in one cell: give `columns`, `lowers`, and `uppers` one
entry per series, and `colors` and `labels` to key them in a footer legend.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Term: ["Headache", "Nausea", "Fatigue"],
    D1: [2.1, -1.4, 3.3], L1: [-1.0, -4.2, 0.1], U1: [5.2, 1.4, 6.5],
    D2: [-0.5, 0.8, 1.2], L2: [-3.6, -2.1, -1.9], U2: [2.6, 3.7, 4.3]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "hide", columns: ["L1", "U1", "D2", "L2", "U2"] },
    { type: "errorbar",
      columns: ["D1", "D2"], lowers: ["L1", "L2"], uppers: ["U1", "U2"],
      colors: ["#5b8ff9", "#f6903d"], labels: ["Drug A", "Drug B"],
      min: -5, max: 7, ref: 0, axis: true, axis_label: "Risk difference (%)" }
  ]
});
```

### Sparklines {#sec:js-sparkline}

`sparkline` draws a per-row series as a small line or bar chart. `columns` is
either a single list-column (each cell a numeric array) or several numeric
columns read across the row (hide all but the first). `kind` is `"line"`
(default) or `"bar"`, `color` styles the line or bars, and `min` and `max` set a
shared vertical scale (by default each row scales to its own range).

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    City: ["Oslo", "Cairo", "Lima"],
    Temp: [[-3, -2, 1, 6, 12, 16], [14, 15, 18, 23, 28, 31], [19, 19, 18, 16, 15, 15]],
    Rain: [[49, 36, 47, 41, 53, 60], [5, 4, 4, 1, 0, 0], [8, 4, 2, 1, 1, 1]]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "sparkline", columns: ["Temp"] },
    { type: "sparkline", columns: ["Rain"], kind: "bar", color: "#4caf50" }
  ]
});
```

### Dot plots {#sec:js-dotplot}

`dotplot` puts one dot per column on a shared scale, so a row with N columns
shows N dots laid out by value. `columns` lists the value columns (hide all but
the first), `colors` gives one color per column, and `labels` names them in a
footer legend (the column names by default). `min`, `max`, `axis`, and
`axis_label` work as for error bars. Since the cell shows every column, label
its header with all the names joined, using a `label` op.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Group:  ["Control", "Low", "High"],
    Before: [3.1, 3.4, 3.0],
    After:  [3.3, 4.1, 5.2]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "hide", columns: ["After"] },
    { type: "label", labels: { Before: "Before / After" } },
    { type: "dotplot", columns: ["Before", "After"],
      colors: ["#999999", "#1a9641"], labels: ["Baseline", "Follow-up"],
      min: 2.5, max: 5.5, axis: true, axis_label: "Score" }
  ]
});
```

`stagger: true` spreads near-equal dots onto separate tracks so they do not
overlap, and the cell grows taller to fit one track per column:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Group:  ["Control", "Low", "High"],
    Before: [3.1, 3.4, 3.0],
    After:  [3.2, 4.1, 5.2]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "hide", columns: ["After"] },
    { type: "label", labels: { Before: "Before / After" } },
    { type: "dotplot", columns: ["Before", "After"], stagger: true,
      colors: ["#999999", "#1a9641"], labels: ["Baseline", "Follow-up"],
      min: 2.5, max: 5.5, axis: true, axis_label: "Score" }
  ]
});
```

## Row groups and indentation {#sec:js-groups}

### Grouping by a column {#sec:js-group}

`row_group` takes a column name or an array of names. An array of one name
groups by that column's values, shown as rowspan cells on the left:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Region: ["East", "East", "West", "West", "West"],
    City: ["New York", "Boston", "Seattle", "Portland", "Denver"],
    Population: [8336817, 675647, 737015, 652503, 715522]
  },
  row_group: ["Region"]
});
```

When the column is character and any value is longer than 20 characters, a
single-column group switches to separator rows on its own, since long labels
squeeze a rowspan cell:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Department: ["Cardiovascular Research", "Cardiovascular Research",
                 "Biostatistics", "Biostatistics"],
    Trial: ["ATLAS-2", "BEACON", "PRIME-1", "NEXUS"],
    N: [450, 320, 280, 510]
  },
  row_group: ["Department"]
});
```

Set `auto_sep: false` to force rowspan mode:

```{js}
// Force rowspan mode by disabling auto-detection
LT.build({
  data: {
    Department: ["Cardiovascular Research", "Cardiovascular Research",
                 "Biostatistics", "Biostatistics"],
    Trial: ["ATLAS-2", "BEACON", "PRIME-1", "NEXUS"],
    N: [450, 320, 280, 510]
  },
  row_group: ["Department"],
  auto_sep: false
});
```

Several columns nest as hierarchical rowspan cells:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Region: ["East", "East", "East", "West", "West", "West"],
    State: ["NY", "NY", "MA", "WA", "WA", "OR"],
    City: ["New York", "Buffalo", "Boston", "Seattle", "Spokane", "Portland"],
    Population: [8336817, 278349, 675647, 737015, 228989, 652503]
  },
  row_group: ["Region", "State"]
});
```

Pass a plain string (rather than an array) to always use separator rows:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    arm: ["Placebo", "Placebo", "Treatment", "Treatment"],
    stat: ["n", "Mean", "n", "Mean"],
    value: [30, 4.2, 31, 6.8]
  },
  row_group: "arm"
});
```

A `group_order` op reorders separator groups:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    arm: ["Placebo", "Placebo", "Treatment", "Treatment"],
    stat: ["n", "Mean", "n", "Mean"],
    value: ["30", "4.2", "31", "6.8"]
  },
  row_group: "arm",
  ops: [
    { type: "group_order", order: ["Treatment", "Placebo"] }
  ]
});
```

### Manual groups {#sec:js-manual-group}

Define groups by hand, with 1-based row indices, using `row_group` ops:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: mtcars,
  ops: [
    { type: "row_group", label: "First three", rows: [1, 2, 3] },
    { type: "row_group", label: "Last three", rows: [4, 5, 6] }
  ]
});
```

### Indentation {#sec:js-indent}

An `indent` op nests rows to show hierarchy:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    label: ["Any AE", "SOC: Cardiac", "Tachycardia", "Bradycardia", "SOC: GI", "Nausea"],
    n_pct: ["45 (67%)", "30 (45%)", "15 (22%)", "18 (27%)", "20 (30%)", "12 (18%)"]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "indent", rows: [2, 5], level: 1 },
    { type: "indent", rows: [3, 4, 6], level: 2 }
  ]
});
```

## Styling {#sec:js-style}

### Styling cells {#sec:js-style-cells}

A `style` op applies CSS to cells chosen by `columns` and/or 1-based `rows`:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Endpoint: ["Primary", "Secondary", "Exploratory"],
    HR: [0.62, 0.79, 0.91],
    P: [0.001, 0.042, 0.38]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["HR"], decimals: 2 },
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["P"], decimals: 3 },
    { type: "style", columns: ["P"], rows: [1, 2], css: "font-weight:bold;color:#06c" },
    { type: "style", columns: ["HR"], rows: [1], css: "background:#e8f4e8;border-bottom:2px solid #4a4" }
  ]
});
```

### Conditional styling {#sec:js-style-test}

Give `test` a JavaScript function and the style applies where it returns true.
The function receives the raw (pre-format) value. Use `class` to assign a CSS
class instead of inline `css`:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Endpoint: ["Primary", "Secondary", "Exploratory"],
    HR: [0.62, 0.79, 1.05],
    P: [0.001, 0.042, 0.38]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["HR", "P"], decimals: 3 },
    { type: "style", columns: ["HR"], test: v => v < 1, class: "good" },
    { type: "style", columns: ["P"], test: v => v < 0.05, css: "font-weight:bold" }
  ]
});
```

```{css}
.lt-table .good { color: green; }
```

Leave out `columns` to test every cell, such as to highlight missing values:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    arm: ["Treatment", "Control", "Treatment"],
    n: [30, null, 28],
    response: [0.67, null, 0.71]
  },
  ops: [
    { type: "style", test: v => v == null, class: "na" }
  ]
});
```

```{css}
.lt-table .na { background: #fee; }
```

### Scoping a style to one table {#sec:js-scope}

A top-level `class` (a string or an array of names) lands on the table's
container, so a stylesheet can target one table and not every lt table on the
page. Here the container is tagged `striped`, and a rule keyed on `.striped`
zebra-stripes this table alone:

```{js}
LT.build({ data: mtcars, class: "striped" });
```

```{css}
.striped tbody tr:nth-child(even) td { background: #f2f6ff; }
```

## HTML content {#sec:js-html}

Everything is HTML-escaped by default, so `<`, `>`, and `&` show as typed. Two
mechanisms opt into raw HTML:

- Body cells: set `html_cols` to `true` (all columns) or an array of column
  names, and those cells are emitted verbatim.
- Text fields (title, subtitle, column and spanner labels, footnote and note
  text): pass a one-element array instead of a string. `"<b>x</b>"` is escaped;
  `["<b>x</b>"]` is raw. This is what R's `I()` becomes in the JSON.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Package: [
      "<a href='https://cran.r-project.org/package=lt'>lt</a>",
      "<a href='https://cran.r-project.org/package=xfun'>xfun</a>"
    ],
    Status: ["<b style='color:#090'>stable</b>", "<i>active</i>"]
  },
  html_cols: ["Package", "Status"],
  header: { title: ["Packages <sup>&#9733;</sup>"] },
  ops: [
    { type: "label", labels: { Package: ["Name<sup>*</sup>"] } }
  ],
  notes: [["See <a href='https://yihui.org/'>the author</a>."]]
});
```

## Footnotes and source notes {#sec:js-notes}

Footnotes are de-duplicated by text and numbered automatically. Each one has a
`location` whose `type` picks a region: `title` (with `group: "title"` or
`group: "subtitle"`), `column_labels`, `column_spanners`, `row_groups`, or
`body`. The example attaches one to every kind of place:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Arm: ["Treatment", "Treatment", "Control", "Control"],
    Stat: ["n", "Mean", "n", "Mean"],
    Value: [31, 6.8, 30, 4.2],
    SE: [null, 0.42, null, 0.38]
  },
  row_group: "Arm",
  header: { title: "Study Results", subtitle: "Two arms" },
  spanners: [{ label: "Summary", columns: ["Value", "SE"] }],
  footnotes: [
    // title and subtitle share type "title", distinguished by group
    { text: "Source: simulated trial data.", location: { type: "title", group: "title" } },
    { text: "Intention-to-treat population.", location: { type: "title", group: "subtitle" } },
    // a column label
    { text: "Standard error of the mean.", location: { type: "column_labels", columns: ["SE"] } },
    // a spanner label
    { text: "Per-arm summary statistics.", location: { type: "column_spanners", spanners: ["Summary"] } },
    // a row-group label
    { text: "Received active drug.", location: { type: "row_groups", match: "exact", values: ["Treatment"] } },
    // specific body cells (columns + 1-based rows)
    { text: "SE undefined for counts.", location: { type: "body", columns: ["SE"], rows: [1, 3] } }
  ]
});
```

`notes` are unnumbered source lines below the footnotes:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: mtcars,
  notes: ["Data from the 1974 Motor Trend US magazine."]
});
```

## A complete example {#sec:js-complete}

Several features working together in one spec:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: {
    Group: ["Treatment", "Treatment", "Control", "Control"],
    Endpoint: ["Primary", "Secondary", "Primary", "Secondary"],
    Estimate: [0.6123, 0.7891, 0.4567, 0.5432],
    CI_Lower: [0.4012, 0.5678, 0.2345, 0.321],
    CI_Upper: [0.8234, 1.0104, 0.6789, 0.7654],
    P_Value: [0.0012, 0.0456, 0.1234, 0.2345]
  },
  row_group: "Group",
  header: {
    title: "Study Results",
    subtitle: "Primary and secondary endpoints"
  },
  spanners: [
    { label: "95% CI", columns: ["CI_Lower", "CI_Upper"] }
  ],
  ops: [
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["Estimate", "CI_Lower", "CI_Upper"], decimals: 3 },
    { type: "fmt_number", columns: ["P_Value"], decimals: 4 },
    { type: "style", columns: ["P_Value"], rows: [1, 3], css: "font-weight:bold" }
  ],
  footnotes: [
    { text: "Two-sided p-value from log-rank test.", location: { type: "column_labels", columns: ["P_Value"] } }
  ]
});
```

## Interactive tables {#sec:js-interactive}

With `lt-interactive.js` on the page, a spec carrying an `interactive` object
gets the requested controls. Every field is optional. @tab:js-interactive lists
them; the rest of the section explains each.

:::: {.table #tab:js-interactive}
::: caption
[ ](#@tab:js-interactive) Fields of `interactive`.
:::

| Field | Controls |
|----|----------------------------------------------|
| `sort` | Click-to-sort headers and an initial order. |
| `search` | The search box. |
| `filter` | Per-column filters. |
| `pager` | Page sizes. |
| `resize` | Dragging column edges. |
| `hide` | The column-visibility menu. |
| `detail` | Expandable row detail. |
| `profile` | A mini chart of each column. |
| `download` | A CSV download button. |
::::

### Sorting {#sec:js-sort}

Headers sort on click: ascending, then descending, then back to unsorted.
Shift-click adds a column as a tie-breaker. An array requests an initial order,
each element a column name, `"-name"` for descending, or a `{ col, dir }`
object. `false` turns sorting off.

### Searching {#sec:js-search}

The search box matches any cell, case-insensitively, against the displayed text
(`false` hides it). It also reads plain language:

- A condition names a column (by name or label, spaces allowed), then an
  operator: `over` / `above` / `more than`, `under` / `below` / `less than`,
  `at least`, `at most`, `between 5 and 10`, `is` / `equals`, `is not`,
  `contains`, or `does not contain` (the column name is optional for the last).
- Join conditions with `and`, `,`, or `;`; use `or` for alternatives. `and`
  binds tighter, so `cyl is 4 or cyl is 6` and `mpg over 25, cyl is 4` both do
  what they look like.
- A term that mentions `x`, such as `x > 20`, is evaluated as a JavaScript
  expression on the raw cell value.
- Anything else is searched as typed, and a quoted phrase stays whole.

The box echoes how it read your query, and its placeholder and dropdown offer
random example queries built from the table's own values.

### Filters {#sec:js-filter}

`filter` is `{ default, cols }`. `default` applies to every visible column
left unnamed, and `cols` maps a column to its own spec. A spec is one of:

- `true`: a plain box, matching that column the way the search does.
- `{ type: "select" }`: a dropdown that keeps one chosen value.
- `{ type: "range" }`: a two-thumb slider.
- `{ type: "checklist" }`: a popover of checkboxes that keeps every checked
  value (all checked means no filter).
- `{ type: "auto" }`: picks the control from the data. Numbers get a slider (a
  plain box if constant), strings with at most 10 distinct values get a
  checklist, anything else gets a box.
- `false`: no filter for that column, even under a default.

Choices and ends are read from the column, or set with `choices`, or `min` and
`max`; `selected` seeds the dropdown's value or the checklist's checked set. So
`{ default: true }` boxes every column, `{ cols: { mpg: true } }` boxes one, and
`{ cols: { cyl: { type: "select" } } }` gives `cyl` a dropdown.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: mtcars,
  interactive: { filter: { cols: { mpg: true } }, pager: [3, 6, 0], resize: true }
});
```

Typed filters: a dropdown on `cyl`, a range slider on `wt`, a checklist on `hp`,
and a plain box for the rest. A typed filter on a hidden column has no header
to sit under, so it moves into the control bar as a labeled chip (click anywhere
on the chip to open it). Here `gear` is hidden yet still filterable.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: mtcars,
  interactive: {
    search: false, pager: 6,
    hide: { hidden: ["gear"] },
    filter: { default: true, cols: {
      cyl: { type: "select" }, wt: { type: "range" }, hp: { type: "checklist" },
      gear: { type: "select" }
    } }
  }
});
```

With `{ type: "auto" }` as the default, each column gets the control that suits
its data, a slider for the numbers and a checklist for `Species`:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: iris,
  interactive: { search: false, pager: 5, filter: { default: { type: "auto" } } }
});
```

A column mapped to `false` gets no filter even under the `"auto"` default. Here
`Species` is left out:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: iris,
  interactive: {
    search: false, pager: 5,
    filter: { default: { type: "auto" }, cols: { Species: false } }
  }
});
```

A range slider updates its readout as you drag but applies the filter on
release, so the table does not reflow under your cursor. Focus a thumb to use
the keyboard: arrows step it, `Home` and `End` jump to the ends. With `min`,
`max`, and `step` omitted, they come from the data as round, data-bracketing
values.

### Paging {#sec:js-pager}

`pager` is an array of page sizes to offer, the first being the initial size;
`0` means every row on one page. Omit it for the default sizes, or set `false`
to show all rows with no pager.

### Resizing and hiding columns {#sec:js-resize}

`resize: true` lets readers drag a column's right edge (double-click the edge to
fit the column to its content). `hide` adds an eye button at the start of the
search row that opens a checklist of every column by its displayed label.
`hide: true` starts with all shown; `{ hidden: [...] }` starts the named columns
hidden, though all stay listed so any can be toggled back.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: mtcars,
  interactive: { hide: { hidden: ["hp", "wt"] }, pager: 5 }
});
```

### Row detail {#sec:js-detail}

`detail` adds an expand caret to each row and builds a table below it on first
expand. Give an array of column names for a one-row table of their displayed
values (hidden columns included), or a function `(row, index, display) => spec`
(or the name of a global one) that returns the spec. `row` holds the raw values
and `display` the formatted text, both keyed by column name and covering every
column. The returned spec is an ordinary table spec, so it can carry its own
`interactive` field to make the detail table sortable, filterable, or paged.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: iris,
  ops: [{ type: "hide", columns: ["Petal.Length", "Petal.Width"] }],
  interactive: { pager: false, detail: ["Petal.Length", "Petal.Width"] }
});
```

### Profiles {#sec:js-profile}

`profile` draws a mini chart of each column, a histogram for numbers and dates
or a bar per category for text, with summary statistics as a tooltip. The bars
highlight the rows the filters keep. `"header"` puts it in the column header,
`"filter"` in the filter popover (only for columns that have one).

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: mtcars,
  interactive: { profile: "header", pager: 5 }
});
```

### Downloading the view {#sec:js-download}

`download` adds a button that saves the current view (every row the filters and
search keep, in sort order, across all pages) as a CSV file of the displayed
text. `true` picks a default file name; a string sets it. Filter or sort first,
and the file follows:

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: mtcars,
  interactive: { download: "cars.csv", filter: { default: true }, pager: 5 }
});
```

### Row structure {#sec:js-structure}

Sorting and filtering happen within each group or subtree, never across it. A
separator group whose rows all filter out drops its header; a rowspan group
reorders its blocks when its header is clicked and stays nested with several
columns. An `indent` op sorts siblings under each parent and keeps a match's
ancestors visible. Spanners, styles, and footnotes are no obstacle.

```{js}
LT.build({
  data: mtcars,
  row_group: ["cyl"],
  interactive: { pager: [8] }
});
```

### Raw values {#sec:js-raw}

Formatting changes what you see, not what is stored. Hover over a cell to see its
original value in a tooltip, `Alt + Click` a table to reveal all of its raw
values, or `Alt + Double-Click` to toggle raw values for every table on the
page.

## Rendering on demand {#sec:js-render}

`LT.build()` renders the table where its `<script>` sits, so it has to run while
the page is parsing. `LT.render(element, spec)` has no such constraint: it
renders into a container whenever you call it and returns the table element.
Interactive tables built this way are enhanced like any other, so a table can be
built lazily, say only when the reader asks:

```{js}
const box = document.createElement("div"), btn = document.createElement("button");
btn.textContent = "Build a table";
btn.onclick = () => {
  LT.render(box, { data: iris, interactive: { pager: [3] } });
  btn.disabled = true;
};
document.currentScript.after(box);
document.currentScript.after(btn);
```

## Driving a table from outside {#sec:js-control}

Every enhanced table carries a small controller at `el._lt`, so widgets outside
the table, such as a dropdown or a range slider, can filter it without the
built-in boxes:

- `el._lt.filter(id, func)` registers a predicate `func(row)` under `id`, where
  `row` holds the row's raw values keyed by column; the rows kept are those for
  which `func` returns a truthy value. Call it again with the same `id` to
  replace the predicate, or with a `null` `func` to remove it. Predicates from
  every id, together with the built-in column filters and the search, combine
  with AND.
- `el._lt.refresh()` re-renders the body. `filter()` calls it for you, so you
  rarely need it directly.
- `el._lt.view()` returns the current view as 1-based original row indices
  (every row the filters and search keep, in sort order, across all pages),
  which is what a "download what is shown" button reads.
- `el._lt.spec` and `el._lt.state` are there for reading. A widget can read
  `el._lt.spec.data[col]` to build its choices: the unique categories for a
  dropdown, the min and max for a slider.

Predicates live in the table's state, so they survive sorting and paging. Here
an outside `<select>` filters the table by `Species`:

```{js}
// wire the widget up once the page (and lt.js) has loaded
const host = document.createElement("div");
document.currentScript.after(host);
addEventListener("load", () => {
  const t = LT.render(host, { data: iris, interactive: { search: false, pager: [5] } });
  const sel = document.createElement("select");
  sel.innerHTML = '<option value="">All species</option>' +
    [...new Set(t._lt.spec.data.Species)].map(s => `<option>${s}</option>`).join("");
  sel.onchange = () => t._lt.filter(
    "species", sel.value ? row => row.Species === sel.value : null
  );
  t.before(sel);
});
```

## Server mode {#sec:server}

When there are too many rows to ship, a table can ask a server for them
instead. Load `lt-server.js` before `lt-interactive.js`, and set
`interactive.data_url`. `lt_serve()` in R does exactly this (see @sec:serve),
and any server that speaks the protocol below can feed a table, such as one
backed by a database or Parquet files.

`spec.data` only needs the column names (empty arrays will do), because the
first page is fetched too. Optional fields: `data_times` lists date-time
columns (sent as ISO 8601 strings), `data_n` is the number of rows in the whole
data, and `data_cols` holds per-column summaries for profiles and filter
widgets. Without `data_cols`, columns get a plain filter box.

### The request

The browser sends `POST <data_url>` with a JSON body, using
`Content-Type: text/plain` to dodge a CORS preflight. The body is an object:

- `where`: the rows to keep, or `null` for all. A condition is a leaf
  `{ col, term }` or a group `{ op: "and" | "or", items }`. A `term` that uses
  `x` for the cell value and is a JavaScript expression (`x > 5`, `x == null`,
  `["a", "b"].includes(x)`) keeps the rows where it is true; one that starts
  with `!` or is `x != ...` negates. Any other term is a case-insensitive
  substring of the cell text. If `col` is `null`, the term is tried on every
  visible column.
- `sort`: `[{ col, dir: "asc" | "desc" }, ...]`, most significant first,
  missing values last.
- `page` (from 0) and `size`: the page wanted. `size` 0 means every row.
- `cols`: the visible columns.
- `prof` (optional): the columns whose profile bars are wanted.

### The reply

The server answers with JSON (`Content-Type: application/json`, plus
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` if the page lives on another origin):

- `n`: the number of rows in the view.
- `page`: the page returned, clamped to the last page.
- `data`: the page's values by column, such as `{ "a": [1, 2], "b": ["x", "y"] }`,
  with `null` for missing values and dates as `"YYYY-MM-DD"`.
- `prof` (optional): bar counts over the kept rows, for each column in `prof`.

That is the whole contract. A forty-line server in any language is enough to
put a billion-row table in front of a reader.
